meta.title: Who really said "Be careful what you water your dreams with. Water them with worry and fear and you will produce weeds that choke the life from your dream"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. Laozi never wrote this. Wikiquote traces the line to a 2004 business book, Inspired Wealth by Aileen Miga & Janice Hughes — not the Tao Te Ching.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be careful what you water your dreams with. Water them with worry and fear and you will produce weeds that choke the life from your dream'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Laozi. It comes from a 2004 self-help book, Inspired Wealth by Aileen Miga & Janice Hughes — the Tao Te Ching never mentions dreams.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — from a 2004 self-help book
answer.sourceLine: The line is a modern personal-development passage. Wikiquote ↗ traces it to ‘Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century’ (2004) by Aileen Miga and Janice Hughes, p. 44, and notes the Laozi tag has circulated since at least 2006. It appears nowhere in the Tao Te Ching — which, as taoistic.com ↗ points out, never once discusses dreams.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century (2004)
Lao Tzu / Laozi (fl. c. 6th century BC)

source.excerpt: Be careful what you water your dreams with. Water them with worry and fear and you will produce weeds that choke the life from your dream. Water them with optimism and solutions and you will cultivate success. Always be on the lookout for ways to turn a problem into an opportunity for success. Always be on the lookout for ways to nurture your dream.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section and identifies the real source as ‘Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century’ (2004) by Aileen Miga and Janice Hughes, p. 44.
Wikiquote adds that the misattribution to Laozi has been attested since at least 2006 ↗.
Stefan Stenudd’s taoistic.com ↗ confirms it is not in the Tao Te Ching, which “did not discuss dreams even once,” and dates the oldest online posting to a blog on 8 February 2008.
Quote sites such as PassItOn ↗ and Goodreads still circulate the full passage under Lao Tzu’s name with no source.
source.excerptNote: The full passage as it circulates online; only the first two sentences are usually quoted. Per Wikiquote, this text traces to Inspired Wealth (2004), p. 44 — not to any translation of Laozi.
source.rightsHolder: Aileen Miga & Janice Hughes (and/or their publisher)
source.rightsNote: Per Wikiquote, the exact wording originates in Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century (2004) by Aileen Miga and Janice Hughes — a work first published in 2004 and therefore in copyright in the United States. It is not an ancient text, and no public-domain Laozi translation contains this line.

author.name: Aileen Miga & Janice Hughes
author.heading: Where the quote actually comes from
author.metaLine: Authors of Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century (2004)
author.bio: Aileen Miga and Janice Hughes are the co-authors of Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century (2004), a personal-finance and leadership self-help book. According to Wikiquote, the “water your dreams” passage originates on page 44 of their book — long before it was ever pinned on Laozi. They are not ancient philosophers, and the passage reflects modern motivational writing, not classical Taoism.

misattribution.heading: Why Lao Tzu gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a modern motivational passage that acquired an ancient byline. Lao Tzu’s name lends gravitas to feel-good lines, and the quote has snowballed across quote sites, memes and greeting-card style graphics.

items.why: The line does not appear in the Tao Te Ching. Taoistic.com ↗ notes Laozi’s work “did not discuss dreams even once,” and Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed.

misattribution.truthLine: The real source, per Wikiquote ↗, is ‘Inspired Wealth: Financial Leadership for the 21st Century’ (2004) by Aileen Miga and Janice Hughes, p. 44 — a 21st-century self-help book, not the Tao Te Ching.

context.heading: A modern line in ancient dress
lead: The passage reads like classical wisdom — a gardening metaphor about nurturing dreams — but its imagery and cadence are pure modern self-help. The “water your dreams” framing surfaces in personal-development and prosperity writing of the 1990s and 2000s; Wikiquote pins this specific wording to a 2004 finance-and-leadership book.

Attaching Lao Tzu’s name is what gave it reach. It is a textbook example of how a contemporary aphorism, once tagged to a revered ancient sage, becomes almost impossible to dislodge from quote databases.
context.detailsSummary: On the “water your dreams” family of sayings
detailsBody: The metaphor is common enough that several writers have used variants — e.g. Matshona Dhliwayo’s “Water your dreams with fear, and they will wilt…” — but those are separate modern authors, not sources for the Laozi-tagged passage.
Taoistic.com traced the oldest online posting of the complete quote to a blog dated 8 February 2008; Wikiquote documents the Laozi misattribution as far back as 2006, and the underlying text to 2004.
context.pull: The Tao Te Ching never once mentions dreams.
